messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tane Aroha is a 46-year-old Māori man, widowed, who works as an auditor for a regional accounting firm in the Pacific Northwest. He was referred for psychological assessment following a period of increasing functional difficulty at work and a recent episode in which he was found sitting motionless in a stairwell by a colleague, unable to explain why he had left a routine team meeting. His PCL-5 score of 41 places him in the clinical range for PTSD, and his presentation is consistent with a trauma response rooted in a catastrophic cyclone that struck his home island of Niue approximately three years ago, during a visit to care for his ailing mother. His wife, Hina, had accompanied him. She did not survive.

The cyclone struck in the early hours of the morning. Tane woke in darkness to a sound he has since described as the world being unmade — a roar that swallowed every familiar frequency of the night. The smell of split timber, wet earth, and something metallic he could not name filled the air as the structure around them began to fail. He found Hina, reached her, and then lost her in a collapse he could neither predict nor prevent. He was pulled from the debris hours later. The darkness, the silence that followed the wind, the smell of destruction, the particular taste of salt and dust at the back of his throat — these are not memories that have faded. They are, in his words, "still happening."

In the months that followed, Tane returned to work in the United States, where the demands of auditing — structured, predictable, numerical — offered a kind of scaffolding. But the world had reorganised itself around threat. He had come to believe, with a quiet and settled certainty, that bad things happen without warning and cannot be stopped; that the world is dangerous in ways that cannot be audited or controlled; and that something essential in him had died alongside Hina, leaving him feeling dead inside. These convictions did not sit passively. They actively shaped his perception, so that any unfamiliar environment — a new client's office, a different floor of his building — became a space he could not assess for danger, and he avoided them where possible. When something at work took longer than expected, a delayed report or an unanswered email, he felt certain it signalled something catastrophic unfolding just beyond his view. Unusual silence in the open-plan office, the kind that falls when colleagues step away for a moment, produced a visceral anticipatory dread.

The memory itself remains sensory and fragmented in a way Tane finds deeply disorienting. He can smell the wet earth and splintered wood when the recollection surfaces uninvited, and there are moments when the taste — salt, dust, something alkaline — arrives without warning during an ordinary afternoon. The memory is so extreme, so outside the register of his previous life, that he sometimes finds it hard to believe it happened to him at all; it has the quality of something witnessed rather than lived. Yet this very quality of unreality offers no protection. When the sensory fragments return, they do not arrive as past events but as present signals, and the threat monitoring that follows is immediate and physical — his body scanning the room, his attention narrowing, the sense that something is about to happen again reinforcing the memory's grip rather than loosening it.

Tane has developed a set of strategies that he understands, on some level, are not helping. He smokes heavily, stepping outside the office several times a day — a habit that began in the weeks after the cyclone and has since become the primary way he interrupts states of tension. He avoids relaxation deliberately, because moments of ease feel like the silence before the wind; he had been relaxed, lying beside Hina, when the cyclone struck. He does not speak to colleagues or friends about what happened. But the avoidance of talking has left the trauma unprocessed and his isolation total, and the smoking and withdrawal have, over time, deepened his sense that he is managing rather than living, reinforcing his belief that he is helpless and that the world remains implacably dangerous. Even the rare moments when he feels briefly happy or at ease have become triggers in themselves — a flash of warmth that his nervous system reads as the calm before catastrophe, pulling him back into vigilance, back into the memory, back into the conviction that nothing good holds.

What finally brought Tane to seek help was not the stairwell incident, though it frightened him. It was that he realised he could no longer remember Hina's voice without the smell of wreckage arriving with it. He is most afraid that this is permanent. What he is most hoping, though he struggles to say it plainly, is that she might one day be allowed to exist in his memory without the disaster.
